The plasma power electronics, diagnostic x y instruments, and reformer assembly were installed adjacent to the engine for real-time monitoring of discharge performance and methane leak response, as shown in Figure 16. Figure 16. AJAX 2802 ULE engine (left) and integrated plasma reformer test configuration (right). The reformer was installed in-line with the engine’s natural-gas fuel feed, and the plasma driver module and oscilloscope were used to monitor high-voltage pulse characteristics during testing. Prior to ignition, the reformer was purged with nitrogen to remove residual oxygen from the lines. The engine was then operated under steady-state full-load conditions while the plasma was cycled on and off to establish a baseline exhaust composition. The engine exhaust was continuously monitored using a Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectrometer capable of quantifying CH , CO , VOCs, and nitrogen oxides (NO ). Plasma activation produced simultaneous reductions in CH and VOCs, 4 a corresponding rise in CO , and a slight decrease in NOₓ, demonstrating more complete combustion 2 without thermal NO penalty. x Statistical analysis of the methane signal provided quantitative confirmation of these trends. Figure 18 shows the normalized methane concentration as a function of time with highlighted plasma-on regions. Each shaded interval corresponds to a period of plasma activation. Methane concentration consistently decreased during these intervals, with signal recovery when the plasma was deactivated. Across multiple repeated cycles, methane reduction averaged between 1 and 2 percent, corresponding to approximately 0.13 percent of engine power consumed by the plasma system. Variations in the methane signal outside the plasma regions may result from changes in other engine variables. This is why repetitive plasma on/off cycles are valuable for validating the plasma’s impact.
